name: List Done
description: 📋✅ means a task or list is complete and verified. It's the combo for 'done, checked off, and ready to go'—the moment when work moves from pending to finished.
meaning: The clipboard shows the list itself; the checkmark shows it's been completed. Together they form the full arc of task closure: you had something to track, and now it's tracked and done. This combo reads as both accomplishment and proof.
examples: finished all the spreadsheets for friday 📋✅
got through my entire to-do 📋✅ feeling productive
seoDescription: What does 📋✅ mean? It means a task or list is complete and verified—showing you had a plan, executed it, and finished everything.

longForm.overview:
📋✅ is the emoji version of closing a ticket or marking a task complete in a project management tool. The clipboard alone says 'here's what needs doing'; the checkmark alone says 'something finished'; together they narrate the whole thing: the task existed, you worked through it, and now it's verified done.

This combo shows up when someone wants to signal not just that they finished something, but that they followed through on what was written down. It's more satisfying than a single checkmark because it proves there was actually a list, not just a vague accomplishment. The combo also reads as more official and intentional—like you're not just saying 'done,' you're saying 'done and documented and accounted for.' It's the difference between finishing and finishing properly.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
📋✅ lands in work group chats when a project hits completion, in personal messages when someone finishes a big to-do list, and in solo celebrations when the sender wants to mark their own productivity. It shows up after 'got everything done for the week' or 'finished the audit' or 'all items packed and ready.' The combo is most common in professional contexts but also shows up among friends who track habits or shared responsibilities.

The combo works as both a status update and a self-congratulation. Someone might send it unprompted to say 'I cleared my backlog,' or it might land as a reply to 'how's the project going?' The sender is saying: I had a list, I executed it, and here's proof.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Avoid 📋✅ when the task is still ongoing or only partially complete. Sending it too early reads as premature celebration and will confuse people waiting on the actual delivery. Also skip it in contexts where completion is assumed or expected—if your job is to check boxes, sending 📋✅ for routine work can read as over-celebrating the obvious.

Don't use it ironically or to mock someone else's productivity. The combo is straightforward about accomplishment and doesn't have a sarcastic register. If you're tired of lists or frustrated with tasks, a different emoji will land better than this one.
longForm.howToReply:
Mirror 📋✅ if you want to celebrate alongside them—it reads as 'yes, that's solid work.' A specific reply like 'that was a lot to get through' or 'perfect timing' lands as more genuine than another emoji. If someone sends 📋✅ about their own work, a simple acknowledgment like 'nice' or 'let's go' keeps it light and supportive.

If 📋✅ lands on a shared project, replying with the same combo signals you're aligned on the completion. If you're the one who sent it and got back praise, a thank-you plus 📋✅ again is fine—it closes the loop on the celebration without dragging it out.

faqs.question: Does 📋✅ mean something different in work chat vs personal chat
faqs.answer: No—it means task completion in both places. The difference is context: in work chat it's more formal (project delivery), and in personal chat it's more casual (grocery list done). The combo itself stays the same.

faqs.question: Can I send 📋✅ for something small
faqs.answer: Yes, but it reads as slightly over-the-top. The combo implies you had a real list and worked through it systematically. For tiny tasks, a single ✅ or just 'done' lands more naturally.

faqs.question: Is 📋✅ the same as just sending a checkmark
faqs.answer: No. A checkmark alone says something finished; 📋✅ says you had a plan, followed it, and completed it. The clipboard adds the 'list' part of the story.

faqs.question: What if I only finished some items on my list
faqs.answer: Don't send 📋✅. It signals full completion. If you finished most things, say 'got through most of it' or send a single ✅ instead. Save the combo for when everything is actually done.

conversationExamples.message: all client feedback incorporated and deployed 📋✅
conversationExamples.interpretation: Someone is announcing that they completed all the requested changes and pushed them live. This is a status update meant to close out a ticket or project phase. The right reply is acknowledgment: 'great work' or a matching 📋✅ from a manager or teammate.

conversationExamples.message: finally tackled that apartment deep clean 📋✅ never doing it again
conversationExamples.interpretation: A friend is celebrating getting through a big, annoying task. They're not asking for help anymore—they finished it and want recognition for following through. Reply with 'hell yeah' or 'that's huge' to match their relief.

conversationExamples.message: got all the errands done before your family comes over 📋✅
conversationExamples.interpretation: Someone is showing their partner they prepared and stayed organized before a big event. It reads as 'I handled my part, we're ready.' A good reply is 'thank you' or a matching 📋✅ to signal appreciation for the effort.

conversationExamples.message: back to school shopping done 📋✅ three kids outfitted
conversationExamples.interpretation: A parent or caregiver is announcing they finished a major prep task. It's both a celebration of completion and an implicit 'we're ready for Monday.' Reply with appreciation: 'thank god' or 'you're amazing' works here.

conversationExamples.message: finally read all the articles from that thread 📋✅ very informed now
conversationExamples.interpretation: Someone is joking about following through on a social media recommendation to completion. It's self-aware and a bit tongue-in-cheek—they're proud they actually did the work instead of forgetting. A reply like 'respect the commitment' or 'bet you learned something' plays along.
